Asymptotic approximation of a modified compressible Navier-Stokes system Thanks: Acknowledgments: The authors would like to acknowledge partial support by the National Science Foundation through grants DMS-1603416, DMS-2006887 (RG), DMS-1813384 (CEW) and (RW). Ryan Goh , C. Eugene Wayne and Roland Welter Address: Boston University
Department of Mathematics and Statistics
111 Cummington Mall
Boston, MA 02215 Email address: rgoh@bu.edu, cew@bu.edu, rwelter@bu.edu
Abstract.

We study the long time asymptotics of a modified compressible Navier-Stokes system (mcNS) inspired by the previous work of Hoff and Zumbrun [4]. We introduce a new decomposition of the momentum field into its irrotational and incompressible parts, and a new method for approximating solutions of the heat equation in terms of Hermite functions in which nt​hn^{th} order approximations can be computed for solutions with nt​hn^{th} order moments. We then obtain existence of solutions to the mcNS system and show that the approximation in terms of Hermite functions gives the leading order terms in the long-time asymptotics, and under certain assumptions can be evaluated explicitly.

76N10

1. Introduction

The compressible Navier-Stokes equations are given by

(1) ∂tρ+∇⋅m→=0∂tm→+[∇⋅(m→⊗m→ρ)]T+∇P=ϵΔ(m→ρ)+η∇(∇⋅(m→ρ))\begin{split}\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot\vec{m}&=0\\ \partial_{t}\vec{m}+\Big[\nabla\cdot\left(\frac{\vec{m}\otimes\vec{m}}{\rho}\right)\Big]^{T}+\nabla P&=\epsilon\Delta\left(\frac{\vec{m}}{\rho}\right)+\eta\nabla\left(\nabla\cdot\left(\frac{\vec{m}}{\rho}\right)\right)\end{split}

These equations model the flow of a fluid with density ρ\rho, momentum m→\vec{m} and pressure PP. We assume that the fluid is barotropic, hence P=P⁡(ρ)P=P(\rho) is a function only of the density. In the present paper, we are motivated by the question of stability of the constant density, constant momentum solution (ρ∗,m→∗)T(\rho^{*},\vec{m}^{*})^{T} to the compressible Navier-Stokes system in three dimensions, which without loss of generality we can take (ρ∗,m→∗)T=(1,0)T(\rho^{*},\vec{m}^{*})^{T}=(1,0)^{T}.

Kawashima appears to have been the first to partially answer this question in dimension d≥1d\geq 1. In [7], he proves existence of global solutions for a general class of hyperbolic-parabolic systems which include (1) and proves these solutions decay in LpL^{p} at a given rate for p≥2p\geq 2. In the course of his analysis, he studies a system with an artificial viscosity term, then shows that the results hold in the limit that the viscosity term is taken to zero.

Hoff and Zumbrun ([4], [5]) study the asymptotic behavior of small perturbations from the constant state for the compressible Navier Stokes equations. Following Kawashima, they prove existence of solutions u⁡(t)=(ρ⁡(t),m⁡(t))Tu(t)=(\rho(t),m(t))^{T} for initial data u0∈L1∩Hsu_{0}\in L^{1}\cap H^{s} chosen sufficiently small for some s≥[d2]+1s\geq[\frac{d}{2}]+1, and find that the solutions decay as ‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖Lp≤C​t−d2​(1−1p)\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq Ct^{-\frac{d}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})} for p≥2p\geq 2. They show that there exists a unique linear, artificial-viscosity system associated with (1)(\ref{CompNavStokes}) given by

(2) ∂tρ+∇⋅m→=12​(ϵ+η)​Δ​ρ∂tm→+c2∇ρ=ϵΔm→+12(η−ϵ)∇(∇⋅m→)\begin{split}\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot\vec{m}&=\frac{1}{2}\big(\epsilon+\eta\big)\Delta\rho\\ \partial_{t}\vec{m}+c^{2}\nabla\rho&=\epsilon\Delta\vec{m}+\frac{1}{2}\big(\eta-\epsilon\big)\nabla\left(\nabla\cdot\vec{m}\right)\end{split}

which can be used to approximate solutions to (1)(\ref{CompNavStokes}), in the sense that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)−G~​(t)∗u0‖Lp≤C​t−d2​(1−1p)−12\|u(\cdot,t)-\tilde{G}(t)\ast u_{0}\|_{L^{p}}\leq Ct^{-\frac{d}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})-\frac{1}{2}}

where G~\tilde{G} is the Green’s matrix of (2)(\ref{LinArtViscSys}). They go further by obtaining decay rates in LpL^{p} for 1≤p<21\leq p<2, and show that the momentum field can be decomposed into an irrotational and incompressible piece, and that the solutions are asymptotically irrotational as measured in LpL^{p} for 1≤p<21\leq p<2 and asymptotically incompressible for p>2p>2. Furthermore if one additionally has (1+|x|)​u0∈L1(1+|x|)u_{0}\in L^{1}, then the solutions can be approximated by the explicit function

‖u⁡(⋅,t)−G~​(t)​U‖Lp≤C​t−d2​(1−1p)−12\|u(\cdot,t)-\tilde{G}(t)U\|_{L^{p}}\leq Ct^{-\frac{d}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})-\frac{1}{2}}

where U=∫u0​𝑑yU=\int u_{0}dy is the total mass vector. The Green’s matrix is shown to consist of diffusing Gaussians which are convected by the fundamental solution of a wave equation, which they call diffusion waves.

Recently, Kagei and Okita [6] extended the result of Hoff and Zumbrun by computing a second order approximation to the solutions of (1)(\ref{CompNavStokes}) in dimension d≥3d\geq 3. Among their findings, they prove that

‖u⁡(t)−G⁡(t)∗u0−∑i=1d∂xiG1​(t,⋅)​∫0∞∫ℝdℱi0​𝑑y​𝑑s‖Lp≤C​log⁡(1+t)​(1+t)−d2​(1−1p)−34\big\|u(t)-G(t)\ast u_{0}-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{x_{i}}G_{1}(t,\cdot)\int\nolimits_{0}^{\infty}\int\nolimits_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{F}_{i}^{0}dyds\big\|_{L^{p}}\leq C\log(1+t)(1+t)^{-\frac{d}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})-\frac{3}{4}}

for p≥2p\geq 2, where G⁡(t)G(t) is the Green’s matrix for the linearization of (1)(\ref{CompNavStokes}), G1​(t)G_{1}(t) is a low frequency cutoff of G⁡(t)G(t), and the ℱi0\mathcal{F}_{i}^{0} are quantities which can be computed with knowledge of the solution ρ⁡(t),m⁡(t)\rho(t),m(t), as well as knowledge of the pressure PP and its derivatives. Their results also show that the solutions can be explicitly approximated by Gaussian functions

‖u⁡(t)−G1​(t)​∫u0​𝑑y+∑|α|=1∂xαG1​(t,⋅)​∫yα​u0​𝑑y−∑i=1d∂xiG1​(t,⋅)​∫0∞∫ℝdℱi0​𝑑y​𝑑s‖Lp≤C​log⁡(1+t)​(1+t)−d2​(1−1p)−34\Big\|u(t)-G_{1}(t)\int u_{0}dy+\sum_{|\alpha|=1}\partial_{x}^{\alpha}G_{1}(t,\cdot)\int y^{\alpha}u_{0}dy-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{x_{i}}G_{1}(t,\cdot)\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{F}_{i}^{0}dyds\Big\|_{L^{p}}\leq C\log(1+t)(1+t)^{-\frac{d}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})-\frac{3}{4}}

if one includes the additional correction factor given by the ℱi0\mathcal{F}_{i}^{0} terms.

On the other hand, Gallay and Wayne ([2], [3]) study the asymptotic behavior of solutions of the incompressible equations in two and three dimensions. They show that one can obtain an approximation of any desired order if one is willing to assume more spatial locality. Specifically, if one chooses 32<μ≤2\frac{3}{2}<\mu\leq 2 and n∈ℤ≥0n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} such that n>2​μ+12n>2\mu+\frac{1}{2} the for initial data (1+|x|)n​u0∈L2(1+|x|)^{n}u_{0}\in L^{2} one can obtain the existence of solution u⁡(t)u(t) and approximations ua​p​p,k​(t)u_{app,k}(t) such that

‖u⁡(t)−∑k=1nua​p​p,k​(t)‖Lp≤C​t−d2​(1−1p)+1−μ\|u(t)-\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_{app,k}(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq Ct^{-\frac{d}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})+1-\mu}

where the approximation terms ua​p​p,k​(t)u_{app,k}(t) are also given in terms of diffusing Gaussians and their derivatives. The key insight is that for each moment that the solution has one can compute a higher order, and hence more accurate, approximation.

We aim to use the tools developed in [2], [3] to extend the approximation of solutions to the compressible Navier-Stokes in [4], [6] to a higher order. To do so we begin with the modified compressible Navier-Stokes system

(3) ∂tρ+∇⋅m→=12​(ϵ+η)​Δ​ρ∂tm→+[∇⋅(m→⊗m→)]T+c2∇ρ=ϵΔm→+12(η−ϵ)∇(∇⋅m→)\begin{split}\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot\vec{m}&=\frac{1}{2}\big(\epsilon+\eta\big)\Delta\rho\\ \partial_{t}\vec{m}+\big[\nabla\cdot\left(\vec{m}\otimes\vec{m}\right)\big]^{T}+c^{2}\nabla\rho&=\epsilon\Delta\vec{m}+\frac{1}{2}\big(\eta-\epsilon\big)\nabla\left(\nabla\cdot\vec{m}\right)\end{split}

obtained from (1) by adding an artificial viscosity term and assuming that the density is bounded away from zero. From the work of Hoff and Zumbrun, we know that the leading order long-time asymptotics of (3) are the same as those of the compressible Navier-Stokes equations, but this model is somewhat simpler from a technical point of view, so we defer the consideration of (1) to future work. For incompressible fluids, the work of Brandolese [1] showed that solutions of the Navier-Stokes equation which initially have finite moments may fail to have finite moments at later times. This problem does not occur if one works with the vorticity. While it is not known if the momentum field of the compressible Navier-Stokes equation has this same property, we avoid its possible appearance by working with the curl and divergence of m→\vec{m}. If one lets a=∇⋅m→a=\nabla\cdot\vec{m}, ω→=∇×m→\vec{\omega}=\nabla\times\vec{m}, and u⁡(t)=(ρ⁡(t),a⁡(t),ω→​(t))Tu(t)=(\rho(t),a(t),\vec{\omega}(t))^{T} and computes the divergence and curl of (3)(\ref{ModCompNavSto}), one arrives at the curl-divergence form of the modified compressible Navier-Stokes system:

(4) ∂tu=ℒ​u−𝒬⁡(u,u)\partial_{t}u=\mathcal{L}u-\mathcal{Q}(u,u)

where we let ν=12​(ϵ+η)\nu=\frac{1}{2}(\epsilon+\eta), I3I_{3} be the 3×33\times 3 identity matrix and where

ℒ=(ν​Δ−1−c2​Δν​Δϵ​Δ​I3) , 𝒬⁡(u,u)=(0∇⋅[∑j=13∂xj(mj​m→)]∇×[∑j=13∂xj(mj​m→)])\mathcal{L}=\begin{pmatrix}\nu\Delta&-1&\\ -c^{2}\Delta&\nu\Delta&\\ &&\epsilon\Delta I_{3}\end{pmatrix}\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ , }\hskip 14.22636pt\mathcal{Q}(u,u)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ \nabla\cdot\big[\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_{x_{j}}\big(m_{j}\vec{m}\big)\big]\\ \nabla\times\big[\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_{x_{j}}\big(m_{j}\vec{m}\big)\big]\end{pmatrix}

We take (4)(\ref{RhoAOmegaSys}) as our starting point, and address the question of equivalence to the original system (3)(\ref{ModCompNavSto}) in the course of our analysis. Our main results can then be summarized in the following theorem:

In section 2, we prove a number of inequalities for later use in our existence and asymptotic analysis. We also introduce an expansion for solutions of the heat equation which we call the Hermite expansion, and demonstrate how it works for related systems. In section 3, we prove that (3) has unique solutions, and that these solutions remain in the same weighted Lebesgue spaces as the initial data. We obtain asymptotic rates for these solutions in weighted spaces, and find our solutions are asymptotically irrotational as measured in LpL^{p} for 1≤p<21\leq p<2 and asymptotically incompressible for p>2p>2. In section 4, we prove results about the accuracy of the linear approximation, and then show how this approximation can be improved if the initial data is appropriately localized.

1.1. Mild formulation

The nonlinear term in (4)(\ref{RhoAOmegaSys}) still depends on m→\vec{m}, and hence we introduce the operators

(7) Π​a=∇(Δ−1​a)B​ω→=−∇×(Δ−1ω→)\begin{split}\Pi a&=\nabla\big(\Delta^{-1}a\big)\\ B\vec{\omega}&=-\nabla\times\big(\Delta^{-1}\vec{\omega}\big)\end{split}

N⁡(a,ω→)=∑j=13∂xj((Π​a+B​ω→)j​(Π​a+B​ω→))N(a,\vec{\omega})=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_{x_{j}}\Big(\big(\Pi a+B\vec{\omega})_{j}\big(\Pi a+B\vec{\omega}\big)\Big)

Note that the inverse Laplacian is well-defined only when we make a suitable choice of function spaces for aa and ω→\vec{\omega}. We will do so below in subsection 2.1, and then obtain estimates for the action of Π\Pi and BB over these spaces.

We can now apply Duhamel’s formula to obtain an integral formulation of (4)(\ref{RhoAOmegaSys}):

with SzS_{z} the surface element on the unit sphere, and some constants bα,ib_{\alpha,i}. Finally, 𝕂ϵ​(t)\mathbb{K}_{\epsilon}(t) is the diagonal matrix having the heat kernel Kϵ​(t)K_{\epsilon}(t) for each entry on the diagonal.

We want to prove existence of mild solutions to (4)(\ref{RhoAOmegaSys}) in some function space and determine the asymptotic behavior of these solutions. We’ll see that the natural setting for our analysis is found in the homogeneous, algebraically weighted Lebesgue spaces

L̊p​(n)={f:‖f⁡(x)‖L̊p​(n)=(∫ℝ3|x|n​p​|f⁡(x)|p​𝑑x)1/p<∞}\mathring{L}^{p}(n)=\{f\,:\,\|f(x)\|_{\mathring{L}^{p}(n)}=\Big(\int\nolimits_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}|x|^{np}|f(x)|^{p}dx\Big)^{1/p}<\infty\}

and their inhomogeneous counterparts

Lp​(n)={f:‖f⁡(x)‖Lp​(n)=(∫ℝ3(1+|x|)n​p​|f⁡(x)|p​𝑑x)1/p<∞}L^{p}(n)=\{f\,:\,\|f(x)\|_{L^{p}(n)}=\Big(\int\nolimits_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1+|x|)^{np}|f(x)|^{p}dx\Big)^{1/p}<\infty\}

We let Wk,p​(n)W^{k,p}(n) be the subspace of the Sobolev space Wk,pW^{k,p} consisting of algebraically weighted, weakly differentiable functions:

Wk,p​(n)={f∈Wk,p:‖f‖Wk,p​(n)p=∑|α|≤k‖∂xαf‖Lp​(n)p<∞}W^{k,p}(n)=\{f\in W^{k,p}:\|f\|_{W^{k,p}(n)}^{p}=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k}\|\partial_{x}^{\alpha}f\|_{L^{p}(n)}^{p}<\infty\}

We also introduce the vector-valued function space 𝕃p=(Lp)d\mathbb{L}^{p}=\big(L^{p}\big)^{d} with norm

‖ω→‖𝕃p=maxi=1,2,3⁡‖ωi‖Lp\|\vec{\omega}\|_{\mathbb{L}^{p}}=\max_{i=1,2,3}\|\omega_{i}\|_{L^{p}}

as well as the function spaces 𝕃̊p​(n)=(L̊p​(n))d\mathring{\mathbb{L}}^{p}(n)=\big(\mathring{L}^{p}(n)\big)^{d}, 𝕃p​(n)=(Lp​(n))d\mathbb{L}^{p}(n)=\big(L^{p}(n)\big)^{d} and 𝕎k,p​(n)=(Wk,p​(n))d\mathbb{W}^{k,p}(n)=(W^{k,p}(n))^{d} with analogous norms. Furthermore let 𝕃σp\mathbb{L}^{p}_{\sigma} be the closure of the space of divergence free vector fields in the space 𝕃p\mathbb{L}^{p}, and let 𝕃̊σp​(n)\mathring{\mathbb{L}}^{p}_{\sigma}(n), 𝕃σp​(n)\mathbb{L}^{p}_{\sigma}(n) and 𝕎σk,p​(n)\mathbb{W}^{k,p}_{\sigma}(n) be the closures in the analogous spaces. Finally, we will make use of Schwartz class functions as tools in our analysis, and hence we will write 𝒮\mathcal{S} for the space of Schwartz class functions and 𝕊σ\mathbb{S}_{\sigma} for the space of Schwartz class divergence free vector fields.

2.2. Heat evolution estimate

In any dimension d≥1d\geq 1, the heat evolution tends to dissipate the LpL^{p} norms of a function. We have

‖∂xαKν​(t)∗f‖Lp≤C​(ν​t)−|α|2−d2​(1q−1p)​‖f‖Lq\|\partial_{x}^{\alpha}K_{\nu}(t)\ast f\|_{L^{p}}\leq C(\nu t)^{-\frac{|\alpha|}{2}-\frac{d}{2}(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{p})}\|f\|_{L^{q}}

using Young’s inequality for 1≤q≤p≤∞1\leq q\leq p\leq\infty and f∈Lqf\in L^{q}. In weighted spaces, one can obtained faster decay under certain conditions described in the following proposition, which is an extension of Proposition A.3 found in [3]. We defer the proof to Appendix B.

Proposition 2.3.

For dimension d≥1d\geq 1, let 1≤q≤p≤∞1\leq q\leq p\leq\infty be Lebesgue indices, let n,μ∈ℝ≥0n,\mu\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be weight indices such that n≥μn\geq\mu and that ∃\exists n~∈ℤ≥0\tilde{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} such that d⁡(1−1q)+n~<n<d⁡(1−1q)+n~+1d(1-\frac{1}{q})+\tilde{n}<n<d(1-\frac{1}{q})+\tilde{n}+1, and let f∈Lq​(n)f\in L^{q}(n) be such that its moments up to order n~\tilde{n} are zero, ie for all multi-indices β∈ℕd\beta\in\mathbb{N}^{d}, |β|≤n~|\beta|\leq\tilde{n} we have

∫ℝ3xβ​f​(x)​𝑑x=0\int\nolimits_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}x^{\beta}f(x)dx=0

Then there exists a C>0C>0 depending only on d,p,q,n,μ,αd,p,q,n,\mu,\alpha such that

(15) ‖∂xαKν​(t)∗f‖L̊p​(μ)≤C​(ν​t)−|α|2−d2​(1q−1p)​(1+ν​t)−n−μ2​‖f‖Lq​(n)\|\partial_{x}^{\alpha}K_{\nu}(t)\ast f\|_{\mathring{L}^{p}(\mu)}\leq C(\nu t)^{-\frac{|\alpha|}{2}-\frac{d}{2}(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{p})}(1+\nu t)^{-\frac{n-\mu}{2}}\|f\|_{L^{q}(n)}

2.4. Hermite expansion

We aim to study the asymptotic behavior of solutions to (4)(\ref{RhoAOmegaSys}) by computing an expansion of the solution using Hermite functions. This is the point where we begin to diverge strongly from the approach of [4] or [6]. We illustrate this process first for the heat equation. To do so, we define

ϕ0​(x)=(4​π)−d2​exp⁡[−|x|24]\phi_{0}(x)=(4\pi)^{-\frac{d}{2}}\exp\big[-\frac{|x|^{2}}{4}\big]

and let HαH_{\alpha} be the α\alphath Hermite polynomial given by

Hα​(x)=2|α|α!​e|x|24​∂xα(e−|x|24)H_{\alpha}(x)=\frac{2^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}e^{\frac{|x|^{2}}{4}}\partial_{x}^{\alpha}(e^{-\frac{|x|^{2}}{4}})

Note that these satisfy the orthonormality property:

(17) ⟨Hα​(⋅),∂xβϕ0​(⋅)⟩=δα​β\langle H_{\alpha}(\cdot),\partial_{x}^{\beta}\phi_{0}(\cdot)\rangle=\delta_{\alpha\beta}
Proposition 2.6.

For arbitrary dimension d≥1d\geq 1, suppose that u0∈L1​(n)u_{0}\in L^{1}(n) for n≥0n\geq 0. If u⁡(t)=Kν​(t)∗u0u(t)=K_{\nu}(t)\ast u_{0} is the solution of the heat equation in C0​[[0,∞),L1​(n)]C^{0}\big[[0,\infty),L^{1}(n)\big], then we can write

u⁡(x,t)=∑|α|≤⌊n⌋⟨Hα,u0⟩​∂xαKν​(t)∗ϕ0​(x)+R⁡(x,t)u(x,t)=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq\lfloor n\rfloor}\big\langle H_{\alpha},u_{0}\big\rangle\partial_{x}^{\alpha}K_{\nu}(t)\ast\phi_{0}(x)+R(x,t)

where for any μ≤n\mu\leq n

‖R⁡(⋅,t)‖L̊p​(μ)≤C​‖u0‖L1​(n)​(ν​t)−d2​(1−1p)−n−μ2\|R(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathring{L}^{p}(\mu)}\leq C\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(n)}(\nu t)^{-\frac{d}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})-\frac{n-\mu}{2}}
Proof.

If we write

u⁡(x,t)=∑|α|≤⌊n⌋⟨Hα,u0⟩​∂xαKν​(t)∗ϕ0​(x)+R⁡(x,t)u(x,t)=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq\lfloor n\rfloor}\big\langle H_{\alpha},u_{0}\big\rangle\partial_{x}^{\alpha}K_{\nu}(t)\ast\phi_{0}(x)+R(x,t)

then we note that the remainder term R⁡(x,t)R(x,t) is itself a solution of the heat equation. Furthermore, we note that at time t=0t=0 we have

⟨Hβ,R⁡(⋅,0)⟩=0\big\langle H_{\beta},R(\cdot,0)\big\rangle=0

for all |β|≤⌊n⌋|\beta|\leq\lfloor n\rfloor. Therefore RjR_{j} satisfies the moment zero condition required in Proposition 2.3, which then gives us our result. ∎

The Hermite expansion illustrates a few of the features of the heat evolution. We note that orders of this expansion decay sequentially faster, and the remainder at least matches the fastest decay rate. The Hermite functions are self similar under the heat evolution, in the sense that the heat evolution acts on these functions by dilation and scaling. See [2] for details. Importantly, the Hermite expansion illustrates how the heat evolution dissipates the moments of a function. The α\alphath moment evolves according to the α\alphath term in the Hermite expansion. For instance, the zeroth order Hermite function gives an explicit example of an initial condition for which the heat evolution preserves the L1L^{1} norm, yet has any degree of algebraic decay one could ask for, and hence the estimate in (15)(\ref{HeatEst}) is sharp with respect to the zero mass condition. However, the L∞L^{\infty} norm decays, so here the heat evolution is spreading mass around, but it conserves the total signed mass. The first order Hermite function provides an example where the total signed mass is zero, and we see that its L1L^{1} norm does decay. The Hermite expansion can be used to show that this holds in general, and similar statements can be made about higher order moments.

2.4.1. Hermite expansion for the hyperbolic-parabolic system

We need a Hermite expansion for the hyperbolic-parabolic system

(18) ∂tρL=ν​Δ​ρL−aL∂taL=−c2​Δ​ρL+ν​Δ​aL\begin{split}\partial_{t}\rho_{L}&=\nu\Delta\rho_{L}-a_{L}\\ \partial_{t}a_{L}&=-c^{2}\Delta\rho_{L}+\nu\Delta a_{L}\end{split}

where e^j\hat{e}_{j} are the standard unit two vectors. We determine these asymptotic profiles explicitly in Appendix D below. We then have the following analogue of the Hermite expansion, where for convenience we assume that ρ\rho has at least one weak derivative:

(ρL​(x,t)aL​(x,t))=∑i≤2|α|≤⌊n⌋⟨Hαe→i,(ρ0a0)⟩ ∂xα(ρi​(x,t)ai​(x,t))+(ρL​R​(x,t)aL​R​(x,t))\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}\rho_{L}(x,t)\\ a_{L}(x,t)\end{pmatrix}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\leq 2\\ |\alpha|\leq\lfloor n\rfloor\end{subarray}}\big\langle H_{\alpha}\vec{e}_{i},\begin{pmatrix}\rho_{0}\\ a_{0}\end{pmatrix}\big\rangle\text{ }\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\begin{pmatrix}\rho_{i}(x,t)\\ a_{i}(x,t)\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}\rho_{LR}(x,t)\\ a_{LR}(x,t)\end{pmatrix}\end{split}

(21) ‖ρL​R​(⋅,t)‖L̊p​(μ)≤C⁡(‖ρ0‖L1​(n)+‖a0‖L1​(n))​t−d2​(1−1p)​(1+t)d+14−d−12​(1−1p)−n2+μ‖aL​R​(⋅,t)‖L̊p​(μ)≤C⁡(‖ρ0‖L1​(n)+‖a0‖L1​(n))​t−d2​(1−1p)​(1+t)d−14−d−12​(1−1p)−n2+μ\begin{split}\|\rho_{LR}(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathring{L}^{p}(\mu)}\leq C\big(\|\rho_{0}\|_{L^{1}(n)}+\|a_{0}\|_{L^{1}(n)}\big)t^{-\frac{d}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})}(1+t)^{\frac{d+1}{4}-\frac{d-1}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})-\frac{n}{2}+\mu}\\ \|a_{LR}(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathring{L}^{p}(\mu)}\leq C\big(\|\rho_{0}\|_{L^{1}(n)}+\|a_{0}\|_{L^{1}(n)}\big)t^{-\frac{d}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})}(1+t)^{\frac{d-1}{4}-\frac{d-1}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})-\frac{n}{2}+\mu}\end{split}

Hence we need to choose a function space for (a,ω→)(a,\vec{\omega}). In the Hermite expansions above, we saw that we could obtain higher order approximations by increasing the spatial localization of the initial conditions. 4. Asymptotic approximations to the modified compressible Navier-Stokes

With these solutions in hand, we turn to the task of approximating these solutions efficiently and accurately, especially in the regime t→∞t\to\infty. If u⁡(t)=(ρ⁡(t),a⁡(t),ω→​(t))Tu(t)=(\rho(t),a(t),\vec{\omega}(t))^{T} is the solution belonging to Yn,k×Xn,kY_{n,k}\times X_{n,k} given by Theorem 2 with initial condition (ρ0,a0,ω→0)T(\rho_{0},a_{0},\vec{\omega}_{0})^{T}, a0,ω→0a_{0},\vec{\omega}_{0} with zero total mass, then we can write

where ρi\rho_{i}, aia_{i} are defined in (20)(\ref{RhoAHermiteProfiles}), and where p→α~,j,f→α~,j\vec{p}_{\tilde{\alpha},j},\vec{f}_{\tilde{\alpha},j} are defined in Table 1. For simplicity, we will drop the nn dependence in the subscript. We obtained the temporal behavior of uL​R​(t)u_{LR}(t) in Prop 2.7 2.8. In the above existence analysis, we saw that uN​(t)u_{N}(t) decays faster than uL​(t)u_{L}(t) in some, but not necessarily all, LpL^{p} norms, hence we need to study uN​(t)u_{N}(t) more closely. We note that uN​(t)u_{N}(t) can be written as

uN(t)=−∫0teℒ⁡(t−s)𝒬(u(s),u(s))dsu_{N}(t)=-\int\nolimits_{0}^{t}e^{\mathcal{L}(t-s)}\mathcal{Q}\big(u(s),u(s)\big)ds

so inspired by (46), (47), we define the Hermite-Picard profiles uH​P​(t)u_{HP}(t) and nonlinear remainder uN​R​(t)u_{NR}(t):

where uI​(t)=(ρI​(t),aI​(t),ω→I​(t))Tu_{I}(t)=(\rho_{I}(t),a_{I}(t),\vec{\omega}_{I}(t))^{T}, I=L,H​P,N​RI=L,HP,NR. We have already obtained upper bounds on the temporal behavior of uH​(t)u_{H}(t) in Appendix E and uL​R​(t)u_{LR}(t) in Prop 2.7 and 2.8. In what follows, we will obtain upper bounds for uH​P​(t)u_{HP}(t) and uN​R​(t)u_{NR}(t), as well as lower bounds for uH​(t)u_{H}(t). Our goal is to emphasize the role that the localization of the initial conditions (and consequently, the localization of the solutions) plays in determining the nature of the asymptotics. In particular, we will establish:

  • •

    For all n>0n>0, uH​(t)u_{H}(t) captures the leading order behavior for ρ⁡(t)\rho(t), but for n≤1n\leq 1 we need to take ua​p​p​(t)=uL​(t)u_{app}(t)=u_{L}(t) to capture the leading order behavior for a⁡(t)a(t) and ω→​(t)\vec{\omega}(t).

  • •

    For n>1n>1 we need only evaluate the explicit functions uH​(t)u_{H}(t) to obtain the leading order behavior.

  • •

    For 1<n<21<n<2 the next order of behavior is given by uL​R​(t)u_{LR}(t), and uH​P​(t)u_{HP}(t) and uN​R​(t)u_{NR}(t) decay faster still. Hence we could either use ua​p​p​(t)=uL​(t)u_{app}(t)=u_{L}(t) or ua​p​p​(t)=uH​(t)u_{app}(t)=u_{H}(t).

    • –

      In the first case, the error decays 1/21/2 power faster than uH​(t)u_{H}(t), hence is more accurate, but we need to compute a convolution (this is the result in Theorem 1).

    • –

      In the second case the error decays (n−1)/2(n-1)/2 powers faster than uH​(t)u_{H}(t) but we can explicitly evaluate the approximation.

  • •

    Finally, for n=2n=2 there is no loss in accuracy by taking ua​p​p​(t)=uH​(t)u_{app}(t)=u_{H}(t).

Appendix A Proof of the estimates on Π\Pi and BB in Proposition 2.1

We begin the proof with the following Lemmas:

Lemma A.1.

For p2,p3p_{2},p_{3} and nn chosen as in part (b) above, and given f,gf,g such that

f⁡(x)=∫ℝ3g⁡(y)|x−y|2​𝑑yf(x)=\int\nolimits_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{g(y)}{|x-y|^{2}}dy

we have

‖f‖Lp2​(n)≤C​‖g‖Lp3​(n)\|f\|_{L^{p_{2}}(n)}\leq C\|g\|_{L^{p_{3}}(n)}
Proof.

The proof is based on a dyadic decomposition

ℝ3=∪j=0∞Aj\mathbb{R}^{3}=\cup_{j=0}^{\infty}A_{j}

C.1. Proof of Proposition 2.4

We first obtain point-wise estimates. Recalling the form of the Kirchhoff formula, we need a bound on the spherical integral of the Gaussian, so we begin with the following estimate:

Lemma C.1.

In any dimension d≥1d\geq 1,

∫|z|=1e−|x+c​t​z|2a​t​𝑑S​(z)≤C⁡(d)​(1+t)−d−12​e−(|x|−c​t)24​a​t.\int\nolimits_{|z|=1}\mathrm{e}^{\frac{-|x+ctz|^{2}}{at}}dS(z)\leq C(d)\left(1+t\right)^{-\frac{d-1}{2}}\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{(|x|-ct)^{2}}{4at}}.
Proof.

We recall the proof given by [5]. First note that the integral above is rotationally invariant so that we may, without loss of generality, set x=|x|​e1x=|x|e_{1}. It then suffices to integrate over the set {z:|z|=1,z1≤0}\{z\,:\,|z|=1,\,\,z_{1}\leq 0\}, since the other part is smaller, and we’ll relabel zz with −z-z for convenience. Note that for such xx and zz,

3​|x−t​z|2≥(|x|−c​t)2+2​|x−c​t​z|2≥(|x|−c​t)2+2​(|x|2−2​|x|​z1​c​t+c2​t2​|z|2)≥(|x|−c​t)2+2​c2​t2​(1−z12)≥(|x|−c​t)2+c2​t2​(1−z1)\begin{split}3|x-tz|^{2}&\geq(|x|-ct)^{2}+2|x-ctz|^{2}\geq(|x|-ct)^{2}+2(|x|^{2}-2|x|z_{1}ct+c^{2}t^{2}|z|^{2})\\ &\geq(|x|-ct)^{2}+2c^{2}t^{2}(1-z_{1}^{2})\\ &\geq(|x|-ct)^{2}+c^{2}t^{2}(1-z_{1})\end{split}

This can then be used to obtain the estimate

∫|z|=1,z1≥0e−||x|​e1−c​t​z|2a​t​dS​(z)≤e−(|x|−c​t)23​a​t​∫|z|=1,z1≥0ec2​t​(z1−1)3​a​𝑑S​(z)=C⁡(d)​(c​ta)−d−12​e−(|x|−c​t)23​a​t\begin{split}\int_{|z|=1,z_{1}\geq 0}\mathrm{e}^{\frac{-||x|e_{1}-ctz|^{2}}{at}}dS(z)&\leq\mathrm{e}^{\frac{-(|x|-ct)^{2}}{3at}}\int_{|z|=1,z_{1}\geq 0}\mathrm{e}^{\frac{c^{2}t(z_{1}-1)}{3a}}dS(z)=C(d)\Big(\frac{ct}{a}\Big)^{-\frac{d-1}{2}}\mathrm{e}^{\frac{-(|x|-ct)^{2}}{3at}}\end{split}

by a simple calculation using the parameterization z1=1−(z22+…+zd2)z_{1}=\sqrt{1-(z_{2}^{2}+...+z_{d}^{2})} of the hemispherical integral. We can improve this somewhat when 0<c​t<10<ct<1. Note that for |z|=1|z|=1, we have

|x+c​t​z|2=|x|2+c2​t2−2​c​t​|x|≥|x|24−2​c2​t2,|x+ctz|^{2}=|x|^{2}+c^{2}t^{2}-2ct|x|\geq\frac{|x|^{2}}{4}-2c^{2}t^{2}\ ,

so if 0<c​t<a0<ct<a,

∫|z|=1e−|x+c​t​z|2a​t​𝑑S​(z)≤∫|z|=1e−|x|24​a​t​e2​c2​ta​𝑑S​(z)≤C⁡(d)​e−|x|24​a​t.\int\nolimits_{|z|=1}e^{-\frac{|x+ctz|^{2}}{at}}dS(z)\leq\int\nolimits_{|z|=1}e^{-\frac{|x|^{2}}{4at}}e^{\frac{2c^{2}t}{a}}dS(z)\leq C(d)e^{-\frac{|x|^{2}}{4at}}\ .

On the other hand, for a≤c​t≤1a\leq ct\leq 1, (c​t/a)−d−12≤1(ct/a)^{-\frac{d-1}{2}}\leq 1, so we have

∫|z|=1e−|x+c​t​z|2a​t​𝑑S​(z)≤C⁡(d)​e−(|x|−c​t)23​a​t\int\nolimits_{|z|=1}e^{-\frac{|x+ctz|^{2}}{at}}dS(z)\leq C(d)e^{-\frac{(|x|-ct)^{2}}{3at}}\

Appendix E Analysis of the linear evolution

We show that ρL​(t),aL​(t)\rho_{L}(t),a_{L}(t) and ω→L​(t)\vec{\omega}_{L}(t) defined in defined by (19) and (22) for t>0t>0 and (ρL​(t),aL​(t),ω→L​(t))T=(ρ0,a0,ω→0)T(\rho_{L}(t),a_{L}(t),\vec{\omega}_{L}(t))^{T}=(\rho_{0},a_{0},\vec{\omega}_{0})^{T} for t=0t=0 map [0,∞)[0,\infty) continuously into Lp​(n)L^{p}(n) for initial conditions in Lp​(n)L^{p}(n), and that these define differentiable functions of space and time for t>0t>0. We also determine bounds on the temporal evolution of the norms of these terms.

E.1. Smoothness properties

Proposition E.1.

(a) Let n∈ℝ≥0n\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, p≥1p\geq 1 and (ρ0,a0,ω→)T∈W1,p​(n)×Lp​(n)×𝕃σp​(n)(\rho_{0},a_{0},\vec{\omega})^{T}\in W^{1,p}(n)\times L^{p}(n)\times\mathbb{L}_{\sigma}^{p}(n). Then

(ρL​(t),aL​(t),ω→L​(t))T∈C0​[[0,∞),Lp​(n)×Lp​(n)×𝕃σp​(n)](\rho_{L}(t),a_{L}(t),\vec{\omega}_{L}(t))^{T}\in C^{0}\big[[0,\infty),L^{p}(n)\times L^{p}(n)\times\mathbb{L}_{\sigma}^{p}(n)\big]

(b) Let n∈ℝ≥0n\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} and (ρ0,a0,ω→)T∈W1,1​(n)×L1​(n)×𝕃σ1​(n)(\rho_{0},a_{0},\vec{\omega})^{T}\in W^{1,1}(n)\times L^{1}(n)\times\mathbb{L}_{\sigma}^{1}(n). Then

(∂xαρL​(t),∂xαaL​(t),∂xαω→L​(t))T∈C0​[(0,∞),Lp​(n)×Lp​(n)×𝕃σp​(n)](\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\rho_{L}(t),\partial_{x}^{\alpha}a_{L}(t),\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\vec{\omega}_{L}(t))^{T}\in C^{0}\big[(0,\infty),L^{p}(n)\times L^{p}(n)\times\mathbb{L}_{\sigma}^{p}(n)\big]

for every 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty and α∈ℕ3\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{3}.

Proof.

We prove continuity at t=0t=0 for part (a), then prove part (b), and the continuity for t>0t>0 follows from the fact that solutions are differentiable in time, and that these time derivatives can be written in terms of the spatial derivatives by virtue of the differential equation that the solutions satisfy. Starting with ω→L\vec{\omega}_{L} we show continuity at t=0t=0 by first noting that it suffices to consider ω→0\vec{\omega}_{0} which is smooth and has compact support by a density argument, together with the linearity of the heat operator, Young’s inequality and the heat estimates in Proposition 2.3. Standard arguments show that for such ω→0\vec{\omega}_{0} we have 𝕂ϵ​(t)∗ω→0→ω→0\mathbb{K}_{\epsilon}(t)\ast\vec{\omega}_{0}\to\vec{\omega}_{0} uniformly as t→0t\to 0, and the result follows. For t>0t>0 one obtains ∂xα𝕂ϵ​(t)∗ω→0∈𝕃p​(n)\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\mathbb{K}_{\epsilon}(t)\ast\vec{\omega}_{0}\in\mathbb{L}^{p}(n) via Young’s inequality and the differentiability as a map into 𝕃σp\mathbb{L}^{p}_{\sigma} follows from the fact that

limh→0‖∂xαKϵ​(t+h)−∂xαKϵ​(t)h−∂t∂xαKϵ​(t)‖L1​(μ)=0\lim_{h\to 0}\big\|\frac{\partial_{x}^{\alpha}K_{\epsilon}(t+h)-\partial_{x}^{\alpha}K_{\epsilon}(t)}{h}-\partial_{t}\partial_{x}^{\alpha}K_{\epsilon}(t)\big\|_{L^{1}(\mu)}=0

for all μ\mu, together with Young’s inequality.

For ρL​(t)\rho_{L}(t) we start with ∂tw⁡(t)∗Kν​(t)∗ρ0\partial_{t}w(t)\ast K_{\nu}(t)\ast\rho_{0}. Again we can assume that ρ0\rho_{0} is smooth and has compact support using Proposition 2.4. For such ρ0\rho_{0} the uniform convergence of ∂tw⁡(t)∗Kν​(t)∗ρ0\partial_{t}w(t)\ast K_{\nu}(t)\ast\rho_{0} to ρ0\rho_{0} as t→0t\to 0 is immediate from the formula

∂tw⁡(t)∗Kν​(t)∗ρ0=14​π​∫|z|=1Kν​(t)∗ρ0​(x+c​t​z)​𝑑S​(z)\partial_{t}w(t)\ast K_{\nu}(t)\ast\rho_{0}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\nolimits_{|z|=1}K_{\nu}(t)\ast\rho_{0}(x+ctz)dS(z)

and from the result for Kν​(t)∗ρ0K_{\nu}(t)\ast\rho_{0}. The continuity in Lp​(n)L^{p}(n) then follows. For t>0t>0 the differentiability follows by the same reasoning as above. The proofs for the smoothness properties of the other terms are similar. ∎

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
